newsitem.title: UK: Britain's Iron Lady is back, but who's she backing?.
newsitem.headline: Britain's Iron Lady is back, but who's she backing?.

text.p: With characteristic majesty, the queen of the Conservatives has swept back onto the campaign trail, yet nobody quite knows who former prime minister Margaret Thatcher is backing in Britain's May 1 election.

Power for her and her alone would probably be the best bet. Seven years after the Iron Lady was ousted from power, she remains one of very few British politicians who say what they believe and stand by it.

No one is quite sure if Thatcher genuinely wants her own Conservative Party to win or whether she would be happy to see victory for Labour under Tony Blair, who has not hidden his admiration for Thatcher's conviction politics.
Conservatives believe she wants her chosen successor John Major to win, only so she can see her own revolution continue.
Others say she wants Major to lose so he can be replaced by a Conservative leader more to her liking and her ideology.
Either way, the signals she sends are decidedly mixed -- and Thatcher is not one to be slipshod over her message.

Publicly at least, Thatcher wants a record fifth win for the Conservatives. She plans at least nine campaign stops and the nation's one-time "nanny" this week marched in to rally the troops, deflated by their double-digit deficit in the polls.
Privately, she admires Blair who shares her autocratic streak and portrays himself as her natural successor with his plan for "radical" centrist rule.
"Margaret Thatcher forced the opposition to face realities in modern social and political life. Ironically, Tony Blair may be the inheritor of her success," said historian Lord Blake.
According to her former speech-writer Norman Stone: "Without the success of Thatcherism, Tony Blair would be unthinkable."
This week, on a pep talk at Conservative Central Office, she bellowed megaphone praise for Major's "magnificent stewardship of the last six years" and urged Britain to vote for more.
A grateful Conservative Party spokesman said: "She's doing her bit, which is incredibly valuable."
But everyone knows this is the same woman who has ruthlessly and repeatedly "handbagged" her chosen heir, saying he lacked the courage to seize big ideas and has "drifted with the tide".
She is dismissive of Major's inclusive nature, his dithering and refusal to be as tough as her on Britain's ties with Europe.
Major fans say the prime minister is simply too decent for Thatcher, yet she remains a goddess to many on the right and an ailing Major is not helped by her sniping.
Indeed, just days before Major announced the election and rallied himself for the fight of a lifetime, Thatcher was quoted as saying a prime minister Blair would "not let Britain down".
Thatcher has called Blair the most "formidable" Labour leader for 30 years: this from a woman who does not praise others easily and who once considered Labour "pernicious".
Blair, too, is keen to cosy up to the woman whose policies he says divided Britain and slashed the safety nets meant to save the have-nots from becoming have-nothings.
"She was a thoroughly determined person and that is an admirable quality," Blair has said of Thatcher.

Blair has even dared to call himself her natural heir, claiming that only New Labour can complete the "economic and social revolution" she began. The Iron Lady begs to differ -- after all there can only be one Thatcher, and she's it.
"He is trying to take over my policies," Thatcher thundered this week, pointing out the need for convictions -- her own.

As for those people who dared see her traits, her policies, her magic in Blair: "I think they have got the sex wrong. I think they have got the willpower wrong. I think they have got the reasoning wrong. I think they have got the strength wrong."
Who could possibly doubt her?
